students.quote:
Charles Spencer Comiter
Charles is a PhD student in MIT’s Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Department, where he is advised by Professors Jian Shu and Collin Stultz. He is broadly interested in developing deep learning methods for the in silico mining biological data that would be otherwise difficult to obtain experimentally . More specifically, he is interested in generating biomolecular data at single-cell granularity from imaging data. Before coming to MIT, he received a BS in Computer Science from Yale University while also taking significant coursework in music. He additionally worked as an engineer for Facebook’s Artificial Intelligence Department for one year.

students.name: Alex Alvarez
students.years_basis: capture_date: explicit own current student-role observation at actual archive/live capture; membership only, no programme/advising start or completion inferred
students.quote:
Alex Alvarez
Post-baccalaureate Student
How do minds generate, pursue, and revise goals across the vast space of all possibilities? How does our environment influence whether we exploit familiar goals or explore new ones? How can dysfunction in this exploration-exploitation tradeoff manifest as psychological disorders?
I’m interested in systems robust to deceptive rewards that sustain open-ended learning. I want to understand how minds avoid goals that appear valuable yet constrain exploration, and instead pursue unassuming goals that later scaffold cognitive structures and expand what can be imagined, learned, and pursued.

Arijit Dasgupta
PhD Student
My research focuses on probabilistic 3D scene perception, with an emphasis on hierarchical, GPU-accelerated probabilistic modeling and inference for extracting robust structure from dynamic visual data. Drawing on computational cognitive modeling, I develop structured Bayesian approaches that integrate motion, geometry, object structure, physical constraints, and uncertainty.
More broadly, I am interested in building 3D perception stacks for physical AI that combine large vision models with structured probabilistic reasoning, enabling systems that are scalable while remaining grounded in uncertainty, temporal consistency, scene structure, and physical constraints.

students.quote:
Sam Hutchinson
PhD Student
I study how we make meaning from language. Beyond our ability to understand everyday speech, we’ve all had the experience of feeling our knowledge expand while reading a book or listening to a lecture—what is happening when we learn from language in this way? This caches out in two more targeted questions: where and how does our language system interface with our conceptual knowledge and semantic memory? What is the representational format of semantics in the mind and brain? I hope to make progress on these questions using techniques from computational cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience. I am also advised by Dr. Ev Fedorenko in MIT BCS.

Zachary S. Siegel
PhD Student
My research goal is to develop robots and AI systems that learn efficiently and generalize like humans — inferring goals, planning, and solving novel problems from limited data. Unlike neural systems that rely on large-scale imitation, I combine Bayesian inference with robot planning to enable flexible, adaptive behavior. I’m working on applying program induction to robotics, allowing robots to synthesize structured “programs” for tasks rather than fixed action sequences — improving generalization, reuse, and interpretability.

students.quote:
Kumail Alhamoud
Kumail is pursuing his PhD in EECS at MIT. He is supported by the Jameel Clinic Fellowship. His primary focus lies in developing trustworthy and adaptable machine learning models. He is interested in designing ways to evaluate models under distribution shifts arising in real-world healthcare applications. Before MIT, he completed his BS in Electrical and Computer Engineering at Cornell University, and his MS in Computer Science at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), where he conducted computer vision research with Professor Bernard Ghanem. You will catch him riding his road bike around Massachusetts in his free time.

Abinitha Gourabathina
Abinitha is a PhD student at MIT EECS. She is co-advised by Professors Marzyeh Ghassemi and Collin Stultz. Her research interests lie broadly in trustworthy machine learning. By investigating the latent spaces and distributions of foundational models, she seeks to audit generative models in high-stakes settings like healthcare and improve model performance for safety-driven goals. She completed her B.S.E. in Operations Research and Financial Engineering at Princeton University with minors in Computer Science, Cognitive Science, Linguistics, and Statistics & Machine Learning.

students.name: Syed Suleman Zaidi
students.years_basis: capture_date: explicit current student role in actual owned section
students.quote:
Graduate Students
Syed Suleman Zaidi, BS
​Suleman is a PhD student at the Brain and Cognitive Sciences department at MIT. He obtained a bachelor’s in computer engineering from the NED University of Engineering and Technology, Pakistan, followed by a master’s in neuroengineering from the Technical University of Munich, Germany. Suleman is interested in using electrical microstimulation and deep neural networks to obtain neural control in the primate visual ventral stream. Suleman is accompanied by his dog Lanai who is also working hard to get her dogtorate.
Weiwen Tian, BS
​Weiwen joined the DiCarlo Lab as a PhD candidate in Bioengineering at the Harvard School of Engineering and Applied Sciences in 2023. She received her bachelor’s in biomedical engineering from Tsinghua University. Weiwen’s current project focuses on visual tasks related to scene understanding.
Coco Yixin Zhang, BS
Coco joined the DiCarlo Lab in May 2026 as a PhD student in Biological Engineering at MIT. During her undergraduate years, she studied bioengineering at UC Berkeley and did neuroscience research at UCSF. She is interested in using computational methods to model how visual stimuli are represented in neural activity.
